summary: A royal psalm borrows David’s victory song to bless God as rock and steadfast love, then marvels that God heeds a mere breath.

context.title: Rock, steadfast love and a breath
paragraphs: Psalm 144 is numbered 143 in the Latin Bible; the Hebrew heading reads of David, and the Latin adds against Goliath. [c1][c2] Its opening strophe imitates David’s song of thanksgiving in Psalm 18, borrowing its titles for God and its image of hands trained for battle. [c3] The Pulpit Commentary still finds original touches pointing to an author, not a copyist. [c4]

Verses 3-4 turn from praise to wonder that God cares for so slight and passing a creature. [c5] Keil and Delitzsch call verse 3 a variation of Psalm 8, using other verbs, and verse 4 a miniature of Psalm 39. [c6] Ellicott suggests the reflection may voice a warrior’s humility, a lament over fallen comrades, or perhaps a blending of the two. [c7]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew calls God tsuri, “my rock”, a title taken from Psalm 18; the Greek and Latin read “my God”.
translationNotes.body: Tsur means a rock or cliff, and calling God my rock repeats a title from Psalm 18. [c8] The Septuagint and Vulgate render it my God, and the King James Version reads my strength, keeping rock in its margin. [c9][c10] John Gill pictures the rock as the place to which the psalmist fled for shelter when in distress. [c11]

translationNotes.summary: God is called hasdi, “my steadfast love”: a bold title that the Pulpit Commentary says occurs nowhere else.
translationNotes.body: Hesed means goodness or kindness, and here God is called simply my hesed. [c12] Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take it as a bold shortening of the God of my hesed in Psalm 59:18. [c13] The Pulpit Commentary notes that the expression occurs nowhere else. [c14] Kirkpatrick, in the Cambridge Bible, wonders whether the text first read my strength or my cliff, as in Psalm 18. [c15]

translationNotes.summary: Hebrew asks why God should “know” a human being, using yadaʿ, the ordinary verb for knowing.
translationNotes.body: The verb is yadaʿ, to know, which Keil and Delitzsch take here in the sense of loving intimacy. [c16] Barnes reads it more plainly as taking notice of someone and regarding them. [c17] Its partner verb hashab properly means to count or compute, so the line asks why God should take account of a creature so insignificant. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: A human being is likened to hebel, a breath: the same word Ecclesiastes uses for “vanity”.
translationNotes.body: Hebel means vapour or breath, and figuratively whatever is evanescent and unsubstantial. [c19] Kirkpatrick prefers a breath to the older rendering vanity here. [c20] It is the word Qoheleth makes his refrain in Ecclesiastes 1:2, which links the psalm to the first reading of the day. [c21] The passing shadow in the same verse draws on the same figure in Psalm 102. [c22]

claims.text: Psalm 144 in the Hebrew numbering is Psalm 143 in the Douay-Rheims and Vulgate numbering.
The Hebrew heading of Psalm 144 assigns it to David, and the Vulgate heading adds “against Goliath”.
The first strophe of Psalm 144 imitates Psalm 18, borrowing its title “my rock” and its line about God training the psalmist’s hands for war.
The Pulpit Commentary holds that Psalm 144:2 has peculiar and original touches that indicate an author rather than a copyist.
In verses 3-4 the psalmist turns from praise to reflect that human insignificance and transitoriness enhance the marvel of God’s care.
Keil and Delitzsch describe Psalm 144:3 as a variation of Psalm 8:5 with other verbs and Psalm 144:4 as a miniature of Psalm 39.
Ellicott suggests that the reflection of Psalm 144:4 may express a warrior’s humility, a lament over fallen comrades, or both.
צוּר (tsur) means rock or cliff, and the title “my rock” (צוּרִי) also appears in Psalm 18:3.
The Septuagint and the Vulgate render צוּרִי in Psalm 144:1 as “my God”.
The King James Version reads “my strength” in Psalm 144:1, with “my rock”, as in the Hebrew, in its margin.
John Gill describes the rock as the one to whom the psalmist fled for shelter when in distress.
חֶסֶד (hesed) means goodness or kindness, and in Psalm 144:2 God is called חַסְדִּי, “my hesed”.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott take “my hesed” as a shortened form of “God of my hesed” in Psalm 59:18.
The Pulpit Commentary states that the expression “my goodness” in Psalm 144:2 occurs nowhere else.
Kirkpatrick in the Cambridge Bible considers it not improbable that Psalm 144:2 should be read as in Psalm 18, “my strength” or “my cliff”.
Keil and Delitzsch take the verb יָדַע in Psalm 144:3 in the sense of loving intimacy.
Barnes understands the verb in Psalm 144:3 to mean taking notice of someone or regarding them.
The parallel verb חָשַׁב in Psalm 144:3 properly means to count or compute, and the verse marvels at God’s regard for so insignificant a creature.
הֶבֶל (hebel) means vapour or breath, and figuratively what is evanescent, unsubstantial or worthless.
The Cambridge Bible renders הֶבֶל in Psalm 144:4 as “a breath, unsubstantial and evanescent” rather than “vanity”.
הֶבֶל is the refrain word of Ecclesiastes, beginning in Ecclesiastes 1:2, and Ecclesiastes 3:1-11 is the first reading on the same day as this psalm.
The image of days like a passing shadow in Psalm 144:4 is the same figure as in Psalm 102:12.
